opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the most important contribution of MaskGAN was less about any single number and more about showing that adversarial training could actually work for discrete text, and why that mattered.

At the time, GANs were producing remarkable results on images, but text was much harder. Words are discrete, so you can't just backpropagate gradients from the discriminator through the generator's outputs the way you can with pixels. Most text generation relied on maximum likelihood with teacher forcing, where the model always conditions on the ground-truth previous words during training. At inference time, though, it has to condition on its own outputs, so small mistakes compound and the text drifts into odd places.

What we did with MaskGAN, working with Liam Fedus and Ian Goodfellow, was frame the problem as filling in missing text. You take a sentence, mask out some words, and the generator fills in the blanks conditioned on the surrounding context. That made the task much more tractable for a GAN, because the discriminator gets a richer, more localized signal about which specific tokens look real or fake. We then used reinforcement learning, specifically an actor-critic setup, to train the generator through the discrete sampling step, with the critic helping reduce the variance of those gradients, which was a big practical obstacle.

The other part I'd emphasize is evaluation. We found that perplexity, the standard metric, didn't necessarily track sample quality. A model could have worse perplexity but produce text that humans judged more natural. That pushed us toward human evaluations and made the broader point that how we measure generative models shapes what we end up optimizing for. That question has only become more important since then.

Looking back, much of the field moved toward large-scale likelihood training with transformers, which turned out to be enormously powerful. But the core ideas, using learned feedback beyond next-token likelihood, in-filling as a training objective, and being skeptical of convenient metrics, have kept coming back in different forms, from masked language modeling to training models with learned reward signals. So I see MaskGAN as an early exploration of some of those themes.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the most important contribution of MaskGAN was really reframing what text generation with GANs could look like. Before that, the few attempts at applying GANs to text were trying to generate entire sequences from scratch, and the signal you get back from a discriminator in that setting is incredibly sparse and noisy. The model gets a single judgment on a whole sentence, and it's very hard for it to figure out which words were the problem.

What we did was turn it into a fill-in-the-blank task. We'd take real text, mask out some of the tokens, and ask the generator to fill them in conditioned on the surrounding context. That did a few things at once. It gave the discriminator a per-token signal, so the generator could actually learn which specific words sounded unnatural. It grounded the generation in real human-written context, so you weren't asking the model to invent everything from nothing. And it made the whole training process much more stable, which was the practical problem that had been killing text GANs.

The other piece I'd point to is that we pushed hard on evaluation. At the time, people mostly reported perplexity, and we argued that perplexity really doesn't tell you whether generated samples read as natural. We put a lot of effort into human evaluation and showed that the samples were actually judged as more realistic even when perplexity numbers didn't favor them. That argument about the gap between likelihood and sample quality ended up mattering well beyond GANs.

And in hindsight, the masked in-filling setup itself turned out to be a surprisingly prescient idea. A year later you see masked language modeling become the dominant pretraining objective, and the notion of conditioning on bidirectional context to predict missing tokens is everywhere now. We were coming at it from a generation angle rather than a representation learning angle, but the core intuition that masking is a very good way to teach a model about language is one I'm glad we were early on.

astra-6.text: I think the most important contribution was showing a practical way to apply adversarial training to text generation. With text, you generate discrete tokens, so you can’t simply backpropagate through the generator the way you can with images. We used an actor–critic approach and framed the task as filling in missing words in a passage. That gave the model context on both sides and let the discriminator provide feedback at each step. The broader idea was to move beyond predicting each word in isolation during training and give the generator feedback on how plausible its own generated text was.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most important contribution was showing how to use an adversarial objective for generating discrete text. With text, you can’t directly backpropagate through the words you sample, so we used an actor-critic approach to train the generator.

We framed the task as filling in missing parts of a sentence. The generator had to produce words that fit the surrounding context, while the discriminator gave feedback at each position about whether those words looked real. That gave us a way to train beyond simply predicting the next word with maximum likelihood, and to explore whether adversarial feedback could improve how natural the generated text sounded.
